content:
A hash table is a way to store information so that, given a key such as a name or an identifier, you can quickly find the value associated with that key. The central idea is not to search through everything one item at a time. Instead, the table computes a small piece of information from the key and uses that to jump directly to a small area where the key’s entry is likely to be. That computation is performed by a hash function. A hash function takes a key and produces an integer, often called a hash code, in a repeatable way: the same key always produces the same code. A good hash function spreads different keys across its possible outputs as evenly as it can, because uneven spreading creates crowded areas and slows lookup down.

The hash table itself is usually an array of places called buckets or slots. The integer produced by the hash function is converted into a bucket number, most simply by dividing by the number of buckets and taking the remainder. If a table has eight buckets, a hash code might be reduced to a number from zero through seven. The bucket number tells the table where to begin looking. When a key and its value are inserted, the table computes the key’s bucket and stores the entry there. When someone later asks for the value associated with that key, the table computes the same bucket again, goes there, and checks the entries it finds. If one of them has a key equal to the requested key, its associated value is returned. If none does, the key is absent.

Different keys can nevertheless produce the same bucket number. This is called a collision, and it is unavoidable in practice because there are vastly more possible keys than there are buckets. A common way to handle collisions is chaining. With chaining, each bucket is not limited to a single entry; it can hold a small collection of entries, often thought of as a chain. Keys that land in the same bucket are placed in that bucket’s chain. A lookup still computes the bucket first, then walks along that chain, comparing the requested key with each stored key. The comparisons use ordinary equality, not hashing, because the hash has only narrowed the search to a bucket; equality confirms whether the particular key is present.

A small invented example makes the process concrete. Suppose a table has eight buckets numbered zero through seven, and suppose, purely for illustration, that the made-up bucket assignments are cedar to bucket three, maple also to bucket three, and pine to bucket six. These assignments are not produced by a real hash function; they are simply chosen to show what happens. If cedar and maple are both stored, bucket three contains a chain with both entries, while bucket six contains pine. To look up maple, the table computes its bucket as three, goes to bucket three, and examines the chain. It compares the first stored key, cedar, with maple, finds they are not equal, moves to the next entry, finds maple, and returns the value associated with maple. To look up pine, it goes directly to bucket six and finds a match. To look up an absent key such as oak, suppose the made-up computation also sends it to bucket three; the table scans cedar and maple, finds no equal key, and reports that oak is absent.

The load factor is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. It measures how crowded the table is. If a table has one hundred entries and one hundred buckets, the load factor is one; if it has one hundred entries and four hundred buckets, the load factor is one quarter. As more entries are added, the load factor rises, chains tend to become longer, and lookups tend to require more comparisons. To keep the table efficient, implementations set a threshold, often somewhere below one, such as about 0.7 or 0.75. When the load factor crosses that threshold, the table resizes: it allocates a larger array of buckets, usually about twice as many, and reinserts every existing entry according to the new bucket count. This rehashing costs time proportional to the number of entries, but it happens only occasionally. Spread over many insertions, its cost is amortized, much as a large occasional repair can be averaged over many days of ordinary use.

The payoff is expected constant-time lookup. If the hash function distributes keys reasonably evenly and the load factor is kept bounded, a typical lookup examines only a bucket with a short chain, a number of entries that does not grow with the total size of the table. Doubling the number of stored entries and doubling the number of buckets leaves the average chain length roughly the same. So the expected number of comparisons remains roughly constant, even though the table is much larger. The qualifier expected matters: it describes average behavior under a good hash and ordinary, non-adversarial keys, not a promise about every single lookup.

The worst case is different. If a poor hash function sends every key to the same bucket, or if an adversary deliberately chooses keys that collide, then chaining does not narrow the search at all. The table becomes one long chain, and a lookup may have to compare against every entry before finding a match or concluding that the key is absent. In that situation the cost grows linearly with the number of entries, so the worst-case lookup is linear even though the expected case is constant. This contrast is the heart of the matter: hashing converts a broad search into a narrow one when the hash distributes keys well, but collisions are still real, and a sufficiently bad distribution can turn the narrow shortcut back into a long walk. That is how the lookup finds its way.
